justification: This is a strong, well-differentiated round 1 that matches the plan's own stated angle for this article almost exactly (CONTENT_PLAN.md row 5: 'Example tests miss a bug -> properties -> generators and shrinking -> build a tiny generator/shrinker -> FsCheck/CsCheck pointer', differentiator 'Tiny framework built from scratch'). The article does not read like the typical top-ranking content for 'property based testing c#', which is either a getting-started walkthrough of FsCheck's or CsCheck's attribute syntax, or a conceptual PBT primer with little runnable C#: this piece instead builds a real, working generator (Gen<int>, biased toward zero/+-1/extremes) and a real shrinker (drop-one-element, then binary-search-toward-zero) from about 80 lines of plain C#, uses it to find a genuine int.MinValue-subtraction-overflow bug in a hand-rolled Sort that seven ordinary unit tests miss, and only then hands off to the two real libraries. The claimed differentiator is real, not marketing copy: nothing about the toy Gen/Shrink/Property.Check framework is copied from FsCheck's or CsCheck's own source or docs (both were fetched and compared; neither publishes anything resembling this specific 80-line implementation), and the running example (Sorter.Sort, then a deliberately half-implemented Median) is the article's own, not reused from either library's documentation or from any sibling testing article. Overlap with the four sibling testing articles is clean: unit-testing-fundamentals owns AAA/Theory/naming/brittleness, test-doubles owns the five kinds of double, test-driven-development owns red-green-refactor, testing-pyramid owns unit-vs-integration -- none of that vocabulary or those examples reappear here, and this article's subject (an invariant holding over an input space too large to enumerate by hand, discovered by search rather than by picking examples) is a genuinely different idea from all four, introduced with its own heading style (declarative/narrative H2s, e.g. 'Why -2147483648 and 1 break the sort') rather than reused templated headings. All six front-matter sources are cited inline in the body -- none of the orphan-source problem the sibling testing-pyramid round 1 review found. The FsCheck instruction was followed precisely: no FsCheck code appears anywhere on the page (only two short attributed quotations), while CsCheck, whose API the writer evidently could and did verify, gets an actual runnable, run-code-verified demo (id=cscheck-demo) that reproduces the same overflow bug with its own real generator and its own real seed/output. The cross-link to /algorithms/binary-search/#the-midpoint-that-overflows is accurate and not a stretch: that section is specifically about (lo + hi) silently wrapping in an unchecked context, the exact same failure mode (silent int truncation instead of a raised error) as this article's a - b overflow, and this article's own ElementTowardZero binary search independently uses the lo + (hi - lo) / 2 form that binary-search.md recommends as the fix, with a one-line note explaining why long is used there for exactly that reason -- a real, load-bearing connection, not a keyword-matched link. No filler intro or outro, no ad code, no keyword stuffing; the toolchain sentence ('Every program on this page ran against .NET SDK 10.0.401 on Windows 11, x64') is the second sentence of the opening paragraph, immediately before the first executed block, not an opening provenance stamp, matching the binding placement rule. `run-code.mjs` passes clean (PASS, blocks=19, executed=7), and I independently re-verified the two most load-bearing quoted claims outside the FsCheck sources -- the CompareTo return-value table and the Array.Sort introsort/insertion-sort-at-<=16-elements remark -- both match their source pages exactly. One thing keeps this out of a higher band and is the reason for the score. The quotation 'FsCheck automatically displays a minimal counter-example' is presented as this article's paraphrase-free quote of the source it cites for that sentence, https://fscheck.github.io/FsCheck/ ('FsCheck Documentation' in front matter). I fetched that exact page's raw HTML directly and it reads 'FsCheck automatically displays a minimal counter example' -- two words, no hyphen. The hyphenated wording the article uses is real, but it belongs to a different one of this article's own cited sources: the GitHub README at https://github.com/fscheck/FsCheck, fetched and confirmed to read '...FsCheck automatically displays a minimal counter-example.' verbatim. So the quoted string is not fabricated and the meaning is identical either way, but it is quoted verbatim from one cited source while footnoted to a different cited source whose own page does not use that exact spelling -- exactly the kind of source/quote mismatch the brief's citation rule is meant to catch, even though the magnitude here (one hyphen, same project, same sentence, two mirrored pages) is far smaller than a meaning-changing alteration would be.
